lecture_context.lecture_title: Lecture 3: Full Cycle of a Deep Learning Project

unit.name: Speed-first data collection and empirical iteration
unit.description: Presents speed of execution as a core tactic for early ML development and distinguishes fast iteration from large upfront data acquisition.
unit.summary: The instructor identifies speed as the guiding principle for early data collection, especially in startups and small innovative teams [ts=979s]. A fast, possibly imperfect dataset collected in one or two days can be more valuable than waiting months because it enables a first model run and exposes concrete failure modes [ts=1033s]. The recommended framing is to set a short deadline such as 48 hours, collect data responsibly and creatively, train quickly, inspect errors, and revise the collection process [ts=1207s]. The advice is conditional: if prior experience or literature shows that a task needs a large threshold such as tens of thousands of images, more upfront data investment may be justified [ts=1393s].

key_points.text: Speed of execution is presented as a strong predictor of success for startups and small innovative teams.
A small, lower-quality dataset collected quickly can reveal what is wrong with the system sooner.
Data collection time should be commensurate with model training time; if training takes hours or days, avoid waiting months for the first run.
Machine learning is empirical: teams run experiments, observe outcomes, and use disciplined analysis rather than random trial-and-error.
Prior experience or academic evidence can justify a larger initial dataset investment, such as knowing a face-recognition system needs about 50,000 images.

kp_catalog.name: Speed-first data collection
kp_catalog.description: Early data collection should often optimize for rapid feedback, using short, responsible data-gathering sprints before large investments.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: Speed-first collection is a useful operational heuristic, not a durable prerequisite concept.

kp_catalog.name: AI projects as empirical systems
kp_catalog.description: AI systems are developed empirically because performance depends on code plus data whose contents and future distribution are not fully known.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: This idea frames the whole lecture: unlike ordinary software, ML projects require build-test-analyze loops because data creates unpredictable behavior [ts=78s] [ts=146s].
